item.description:
Research Experience

Lecturer in Geospatial Engineering
School of Engineering, Newcastle University, 2021-Present

  • I’m a member of the Geodesy research group at Geospatial Engineering, where I conduct research in the field of crustal motion geodesy. Specifically, I am focused on exploring how the solid Earth reacts to surface mass loading.

Research Associate
School of Engineering, Newcastle University, 2018-2021

  • I worked in the UKANET project led by Pippa Whitehouse (Durham University). I used GNSS time series to help infer the rheological properties of the Earth beneath Antarctica.

Postdoctoral Fellow
The Australian National University, Research School of Earth Sciences, 2012-2018

item.title: Research
item.description:
Solid Earth Deformation of Antarctica

The West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) contributes about 10% of global sea-level rise and is losing ice at an accelerating rate. Predicting its future is challenging due to uncertainties in measuring ice mass changes and the impact of land deformation beneath the ice. To address this, I use the Global Positioning System (GPS), which provides precise measurements of the Earth’s surface deformation.
These surface changes reflect various processes within the Earth and at its surface. By using continuously recording GPS stations in the Antarctic Peninsula, I study how the solid Earth responds to seasonal and annual variations in snow and ice accumulation over the past decade.

Solid Earth’s Response to Hydrologic Loading

The Earth is not perfectly rigid; its surface deforms in response to the weight of surface masses, such as water. For example, Earth’s surface sinks under the weight of water during high tide and rebounds during low tide. To track these changes, we use high-precision GPS to measure surface displacements with millimeter accuracy. This allows us to monitor how the Earth’s surface flexes due to the storage and flow of water. By analyzing these GPS measurements, we can estimate the amount of water added or removed from a watershed on both daily and long-term timescales.

item.title: Teaching
item.description:
Newcastle University

Current Modules

CEG3707: Geohazards and Deformation of the Earth

Introduction of active research areas in geohazards, which benefit from the application of geodetic deformation monitoring techniques. I jointly teach this module with Pr. Peter Clarke

CEG319: Geospatial Data, Analytics and AI

Academic Year 2025-2026

The module will explore how modern geospatial data handling, standards, ethics, analysis, simulation modelling and visualisation approaches can be applied help deliver many of the UN sustainable development goals. I jointly teach this module with Dr Alistair Ford
